title: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World
author: José van Dijck · Thomas Poell · Martijn de Waal

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source shifts attention from task-level legal-AI capability, verification and organisational redesign to the broader political economy of platforms: concentrated infrastructural power, embedded public values and democratic regulation. Its context-specific governance approach is compatible with selective deployment, but it does not directly assess legal-AI competence or human–AI work allocation.
qs: Platforms are neither neutral nor value-free constructs; they come with specific norms and values inscribed in their architectures.

The responsibility for a balanced platform society—an open society that anchors its public values in a transparent and accountable manner—rests with all actors involved in its construction: corporations, governments, and civil society actors.

st.t: Platform governance: External innovation preserves gatekeeper power
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s account of platforms as concentrated private infrastructures that govern participation through architecture, data and controlled access. It also affirms that third parties can innovate on platform resources while dominant owners retain control over the ecosystem’s core conditions.
qs: The Western ecosystem is mostly operated by a handful of big tech companies (Alphabet-Google, Apple,  Facebook, Amazon, and Microsoft) whose infrastructural services are central to the ecosystem’s overall design and the distribution of data flows.

By means of application programming interfaces (APIs), platforms, subsequently, offer third parties controlled access to their platform data, giving them detailed insights into user behavior and metrics—information on which they can build new applications or platforms (Helmond 2015; Langlois et  al.

st.t: Platform infrastructure: Convenience can deepen private control
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition by treating platforms as institutional infrastructure that organises social life through concentrated control of data flows, technical architecture, ownership and governance. It also affirms that convenience and apparent decentralisation can coexist with hierarchy, private control and pressure on public values.
qs: Platforms, in our view, do not cause a revolution; instead, they are gradually infiltrating in, and converging with, the (offline, legacy) institutions and practices through which democratic societies are organized.

The Western ecosystem is mostly operated by a handful of big tech companies (Alphabet-Google, Apple,  Facebook, Amazon, and Microsoft) whose infrastructural services are central to the ecosystem’s overall design and the distribution of data flows.

kp.k: Platforms reshape institutions rather than simply bypassing them
kp.d: The authors reject an exclusively economic or technological account of platforms. Against reported claims of disruptive innovation and disintermediation, they argue that platforms gradually converge with existing institutions and actively produce social structures, requiring governments to adjust legal and democratic arrangements. This is a cross-domain theoretical argument, not evidence about AI-driven changes in legal practice.
qs: Platforms, in our view, do not cause a revolution; instead, they are gradually infiltrating in, and converging with, the (offline, legacy) institutions and practices through which democratic societies are organized.
Platforms do not reflect the social: they produce the social structures we live in (Couldry and Hepp 2016).

kp.k: Private platform benefits can impose collective costs
kp.d: The authors frame platformization as a dispute between personalized benefits and corporate gain, on one side, and public interests and collective services, on the other. Airbnb and Coursera illustrate questions about who funds safety enforcement, street cleaning and teaching when users bypass established providers; these are distributive questions rather than quantified cost findings.
qs: While platforms allegedly enhance personalized benefits and economic gain, they simultaneously put pressure on collective means and public services.
Students are tempted to consume “free” courses on Coursera, but who pays for the teaching effort that goes into producing them?

kp.k: Public values are embedded, contested and context-dependent
kp.d: Platforms embody norms through their architectures rather than operating neutrally. The authors distinguish privacy, accuracy, safety and consumer protection from collective values including fairness, equality, solidarity, accountability, transparency and democratic control. They argue that these values can conflict and require contextual negotiation, including when transparency for enforcement clashes with privacy and when US-owned platforms encounter European public values.
qs: Platforms are neither neutral nor value-free constructs; they come with specific norms and values inscribed in their architectures.
The connective qualities of online platforms, however, do not automatically translate into public values.
None of these values are chiseled in stone or uncontroversial; on the contrary, they are the very stakes in the struggle over the organization of platform societies around the globe.

kp.k: Platformization operates through three mutually shaped mechanisms
kp.d: The introduction identifies datafication, commodification and selection as the ecosystem's driving mechanisms. The authors emphasize reciprocal shaping between technology, economic models and users, rather than technological determinism. These mechanisms are announced as the subject of Chapter 2, not fully demonstrated in the supplied excerpt.
qs: We have identified three main mechanisms as driving forces underlying the ecosystem: datafication, commodification, and selection.

Far from being mere technical or economic processes, we emphasize the mutual shaping of technology, economic models, and users: while platform mechanisms filter and steer social interactions, users also define their outcome.

kp.d: The authors report over 22,000 Amsterdam apartments and flats advertised annually in 2018, alongside income and tourism benefits, nuisance, safety concerns, hospitality-sector fairness disputes and affordability concerns amid rising property prices. Airbnb rejected municipal requests for host data on privacy grounds. An agreement announced in December 2016 committed Airbnb to enforcing the city's sixty-day maximum stay limit; policymakers regarded it as a promising first step, but competitors limited its reach. Amsterdam implemented a local licensing register in October 2017, with negotiations continuing at publication.
qs: With over 22,000 apartments and flats per year being advertised on the site, Amsterdam has become one of the popular destinations for Airbnb users in 2018.
Repeated requests from city managers to get access to Airbnb’s host data, in order to enforce local regulations, were rejected on grounds of users’ privacy protection.

However, a deal with the biggest platform was not enough because Airbnb has many competitors, including 9Flats, Wimdu, BeWelcome, Couchsurfing,  HomeExchange, and TripAdvisor, all of which operate under different conditions.

kp.k: Platform governance combines technical, economic and contractual architecture
kp.d: The authors locate governance power in the combined operation of data, algorithms, interfaces, ownership, business models and user agreements. Their analytical framework connects individual platforms, the ecosystem and geopolitical structures, arguing that platforms cannot be understood independently of the infrastructure and political institutions on which they depend.
qs: a platform is fueled by data, automated and organized through algorithms and interfaces, formalized through ownership relations driven by business models, and governed through user agreements.
Deconstructing the anatomy of a single platform helps us understand how its combined elements govern users and user practices.

kp.k: Data collection and APIs underpin ecosystem connectivity
kp.d: The excerpt describes automatic collection of content and user data through devices, software, clicks, cursor movements, social buttons and pixels. APIs provide controlled third-party access to behavioral information and metrics, enabling new applications and platforms. The authors argue that widespread API adoption since eBay's first open API in 2000 helped transform the Web into a data-driven platform ecosystem.
qs: Data provide the fuel for a growing connectivity between platforms.
Since eBay launched the first open API in the year 2000, its ubiquitous employment has arguably transformed the Web into a data-driven, platform-based ecosystem.

kp.k: Opaque algorithms organize visibility and access
kp.d: Algorithms filter content and connect users to services, advertisements and information. Google PageRank and Facebook News Feed illustrate how relevance and exposure are calculated. The authors stress that proprietary secrecy, complexity and continual adjustment constrain transparency; this is an account of platform selection, not a measured evaluation of AI accuracy.
qs: Platforms use algorithms to automatically filter enormous amounts of content and connect users to content, services, and advertisements.
Although platform owners may lift a veil on how their algorithms work, they are often well-kept trade secrets and are everything but transparent.
Moreover, algorithms have become increasingly complex and are subject to constant tweaking.

kp.k: Ownership and monetization shape platform relationships
kp.d: The authors argue that ownership and legal-economic status affect regulatory compliance, taxation and user relationships. They challenge the notion of free services: money, attention, data and user valuation can all generate value through advertising, subscriptions, data sales and fees. Couchsurfing's conversion to a corporation in 2011 illustrates member opposition to changed ownership and monetization; the excerpt contrasts its membership-fee model with Airbnb's booking fees and reported third-party data sales.
qs: Business models in the context of platforms refer to the ways in which economic value gets created and captured.
The “free” strategies adopted by many platforms have resulted in an ecosystem where the default mode is to trade convenient services for personal information (Schneier 2015).
A business model is an intricate part of a site’s philosophy, which is in turn reflected in its architecture.

kp.k: Interface design shapes norms without eliminating user agency
kp.d: Interfaces, algorithms and protocols encourage some interactions and discourage others, but the authors reject treating users as passive puppets. Facebook's expansion beyond binary gender and sexual-orientation categories following criticism illustrates responsiveness to users alongside commercial incentives: richer customer information and changed social norms can result from the same design decision.
qs: Technological and economic elements of platforms steer user interaction but simultaneously shape social norms.

When Facebook received a lot of criticism concerning its binary approach toward soliciting information about gender and sexual orientation, the company responded by including a range of “other” identity options, including the possibility for users to defy any categorization.
Not only did this change make economic sense, eliciting more refined customer information, but it also actively influenced social norms by expanding the conventional binary options.

kp.k: Terms of service function as private governance
kp.d: The authors characterize user agreements as difficult-to-understand, frequently changing instruments that set privacy norms and owner privileges. Airbnb's November 2016 antidiscrimination policy and permission for database background checks illustrate contractual governance. They also raise public-legitimacy questions: platforms respond to public opinion and regulatory demands, while disclosure obligations may remain limited.
qs: These pseudo-legal contracts define and shape the relationships between users and platform owners, but they are often long, difficult to understand, and subject to constant change, which is why many people check the box without even looking at this “agreement.”
Airbnb is under no obligation to unveil what it learns about its user, other than what the company is legally bound to disclose.
platform companies often have to respond to public opinions and react to legal or regulatory demands by adjusting their policies.

kp.k: Infrastructural platforms concentrate power over sectoral services
kp.d: The authors distinguish infrastructural platforms, which manage essential services and data flows, from sectoral platforms serving domains such as transport, health, education and hospitality. They identify Alphabet-Google, Facebook, Apple, Amazon and Microsoft as the dominant corporate core of the North American and European ecosystem. Apparent egalitarianism and customer empowerment coexist, in their account, with hierarchy, centralization and opacity.
qs: Clearly, the platform ecosystem is not a level playing field; some platforms are more equal than others.
Most influential are the infrastructural platforms, many of them owned and operated by the Big Five; they form the heart of the ecosystem upon which many other platforms and apps can be built.
They also serve as online gatekeepers through which data flows are managed, processed, stored, and channeled.

kp.k: Reported concentration extends across advertising and identification
kp.d: The 2018 excerpt reports Facebook controlling 80% of the social-networking-services market and reaching over two billion monthly users worldwide, with Facebook and Google together controlling more than 60% of online advertising. It also identifies their substantial role in online identification and Facebook's expanded reach through Instagram, acquired in 2012, and WhatsApp, acquired in 2014. These are source-reported historical figures, not present-day estimates.
qs: Next to Alphabet-Google, Facebook dominates data traffic as it controls 80% of the market for social networking services, reaching over two billion monthly users worldwide.
Together, Facebook and  Google control more than 60% of online advertising—the dominant component of many Web-based business models.
Facebook and Google also control a substantial share of online identification services (Facebook Login), an important entrance to many other services.

kp.k: Public-value protection requires proactive, multilevel government
kp.d: The authors' normative position assigns responsibility to corporations, governments and civil society, with special responsibilities for local, national and supranational governments. Particularly in Europe, they recommend that governments negotiate public values proactively and adapt regulatory tools, rather than merely arbitrate markets. They present this as an ongoing geopolitical contest, not a settled governance model or implementation blueprint.
qs: The responsibility for a balanced platform society—an open society that anchors its public values in a transparent and accountable manner—rests with all actors involved in its construction: corporations, governments, and civil society actors.

Particularly in the European context, governments are not just arbiters of market dynamics and level playing fields but can and should be proactive in negotiating public values on behalf of citizens and consumers.
Discussing their potential roles, we argue how governments need to adjust their instrumentation for regulation and control to protect a democratically agreed upon set of public values.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Van Dijck, Poell and de Waal argue that data-driven, algorithmically organized platforms reshape social institutions, markets and public governance. The supplied excerpt does not make predictions about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain account of platformization, rather than a study of legal AI. The authors claim that platforms gradually converge with existing institutions, rather than simply replacing intermediaries through a technological revolution. Platform architectures, business models and user agreements organize interactions and embed norms, bringing private benefits into conflict with collective costs and public values. Automated data collection and processing enable more precise and faster profiling and real-time advertising. Infrastructural platforms concentrate power over other services and information flows in five technology corporations. The authors also make a normative argument that governments should adapt regulation and proactively protect public values. The opening claims of automatic empowerment and economic progress are presented as platform promises or other scholars' positions, not unqualified findings endorsed by the authors. The brief reference to Alphabet's AI investments is not an AI-impact prediction.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their claims through a qualitative institutional account, cited scholarship, platform examples, dated regulatory events and descriptive market figures—not AI benchmarks or measured legal-service outcomes.
pts.d: The central example is Airbnb in Amsterdam: the authors report more than 22,000 advertised apartments and flats annually in 2018, benefits for hosts and tourism, and disputes about nuisance, safety, taxes and competitive fairness. They describe a December 2016 agreement for Airbnb to enforce a sixty-day limit and an October 2017 municipal register. Other examples include Couchsurfing's 2011 conversion to a corporation, Facebook's expanded identity categories, and Airbnb's November 2016 antidiscrimination and background-check provisions. These illustrate how ownership, interfaces and terms govern users and norms. Their concentration argument includes reported Facebook social-networking market share of 80%, over two billion monthly users, and combined Facebook–Google online-advertising share above 60%. The excerpt supplies scholarly citations and footnote markers, but not the underlying methods for those market estimates or a quantitative causal test of platform effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern an ongoing transformation from the early 2000s through publication in 2018, with no fixed forecast horizon; outcomes depend on sector, user action and political negotiation.
pts.d: The authors locate the emergence of the platform ecosystem in the early 2000s and describe platformization as gradual and contested. Their main geographical scope is North America and western Europe, while acknowledging globally interconnected infrastructures. They explicitly reject technological determinism: architectures steer interactions, but users also shape outcomes. Public-value conflicts must be assessed in particular applications, social situations and sectors. Amsterdam illustrates a further condition: an agreement with one dominant platform does not govern its competitors. The authors characterize their object as a moving target and present their framework as an analysis of underlying mechanisms, not a blueprint or an attempt to anticipate every development. Later sector chapters are announced in this excerpt, not supplied as completed evidence here.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include platform users, incumbent providers, sectoral platforms, governments and communities; benefits and burdens differ across them.
pts.d: In hospitality, hosts gain income and guests obtain relatively inexpensive accommodation, while hotels face competitive-fairness disputes and residents experience nuisance and affordability concerns. Governments face enforcement difficulties when global platforms resist existing classifications or restrict access to data. Users receive personalized services while becoming subjects of profiling, contractual governance and architectural choices. Sectoral platforms depend on infrastructure controlled by major technology companies. Across news, transport, health and education, the authors identify stakes including journalistic independence, reliable information, safety, privacy, equality, accessibility and democratic accountability. These are cross-domain public-value claims, not claims about law-firm staffing, legal-service pricing or unmet civil legal need. Lawyers appear as participants in privacy disputes, not as a profession whose AI-driven transformation is analyzed.
